stem: After completing contaminated wound care, a nurse must perform a clean task for the same client. What should the nurse do before beginning the clean task?

options.A: Keep the same gloves because the client has not changed
options.B: Remove the soiled gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don clean gloves if the next task requires them
options.C: Keep the same gloves as long as no second client is touched
options.D: Change gloves only when moving from one client to another

rationale: CDC guidance directs healthcare workers to change gloves and clean hands when moving from a soiled body site or contaminated task to a clean body site/task on the same patient. Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. B is correct.
educational_objective: Prevent cross-contamination by changing gloves and performing hand hygiene when moving from dirty to clean care on the same client.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
source_locator: Know when to change gloves and clean hands — moving from a soiled body site to a clean body site on the same patient
source_claim_supported: Healthcare workers should change gloves and perform hand hygiene when moving from soiled/contaminated care to clean care on the same patient.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand hygiene, standard precautions, and prevention of cross-contamination
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — glove changes between tasks

source_original.stem: A nurse is providing care for a single client that involves wound care followed immediately by handling clean linens for the same client, and a colleague suggests there's no need to change gloves since it's still the same person being cared for. The nurse should instead:

options.A: Keep the same gloves because changing tasks for one client does not create cross-contamination risk
options.B: Change gloves and perform hand hygiene before moving from contaminated wound care to clean handling
options.C: Use the same gloves for wound care and clean linen handling as long as no second client is touched
options.D: Change gloves only when moving to another client, not when changing from dirty to clean tasks

source_original.rationale: Gloves should be changed, with hand hygiene performed, between different tasks or procedures on the same client (such as after wound care and before handling clean linens or a different body site), to prevent cross-contamination between contaminated and clean areas or tasks, not just when moving between different clients.
source_original.source_detail: CDC Core Practices: remove/change gloves after a task and prevent contaminated-to-clean cross-transfer; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Removed colleague cueing and anchored the answer to CDC's current healthcare-worker glove-change guidance. Clarified that clean gloves are redonned only if the next task requires gloves. Reduced difficulty from hard to easy.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC Clinical Safety guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.claim_audit: CDC explicitly instructs glove change and hand cleaning when moving from soiled to clean care on the same patient.

distractor_audit.A: Same-patient status does not remove cross-contamination risk.
distractor_audit.C: Same gloves should not bridge contaminated and clean tasks.
distractor_audit.D: Glove changes are also required within same-patient care when contamination context changes.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: B is the only complete correct action.
audit_findings.cueing: Removed narrative hint and tightened alternatives.
audit_findings.blueprint: Standard Precautions/hand hygiene fit Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked CDC current glove-change section; B remains uniquely correct.
